utterance: Hi Daniel, I’m sorry you’re in so much pain. Can you tell me what happened when you hurt your back, and what symptoms you’re having now?
reply: I was lifting a big pot plant in the garden on Saturday, felt a twinge, and then woke up Sunday and could barely get out of bed. The pain is low down on the left side of my back and sometimes goes into my left buttock, but nothing goes down my legs. It gets worse when I bend or get out of a chair and is worse by the evening, while moving about makes it worse and it settles when I rest. I'm a bit stiff in the morning, but it loosens up in ten minutes or so, and sneezing's a bit uncomfortable though nothing shoots anywhere. I've worked from home the last two days mostly lying on the couch with the laptop, and I can walk around slowly. I've tried some paracetamol, but it didn't do much, honestly. I don't have numbness around my buttocks, genitals, or back passage, and my passing urine is all normal with no loss of bowel

utterance: Thanks Daniel. This sounds like mechanical low back pain — a muscle and ligament strain on the left side after lifting — rather than a nerve problem or anything serious. Your examination was reassuring: normal temperature and observations, no weakness or numbness in the legs, normal reflexes, and no signs of nerve compression. I found no red flags for fracture, infection, cancer, or cauda equina. Because of that, an MRI is not recommended right now: for recent back pain like this, early scans usually do not change treatment and can show normal age-related changes. Most people improve over 1–2 weeks, though some symptoms can last up to 6 weeks. Plan: stay as active as pain allows and avoid bed rest; do gentle walking, change position often, use heat, and gradually return to desk work. I’ve prescribed ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day with food for 5 days, and referred you to a physiotherapist. You can also take paracetamol 1 g every 6 hours when needed, up to 4 g in 24 hours. I’ve noted your tramadol allergy, so please don’t take tramadol. Safety-net: seek urgent care or call an ambulance if you develop leg weakness or numbness, numbness around your genitals, buttocks or back passage, loss of bladder or bowel control or trouble passing urine, fever or feeling very unwell, severe pain at night not relieved by changing position, or a major fall or injury. If you are not improving in 6 weeks, or your function gets worse, come back and we can reconsider imaging.
reply: Without a scan, how can we be sure it is not a slipped disc?

utterance: I can’t be 100% certain without a scan, but a slipped disc that is pressing on a nerve usually causes pain, numbness or weakness going down the leg, often below the knee, and it often makes the straight-leg-raise test painful down the leg. You don’t have those features: your pain is local to the low back and buttock, your leg strength, sensation and reflexes are normal, and the nerve-stretch tests are negative. Also, many people without any back pain have disc bulges on MRI, so an early scan can be misleading. That’s why the safest plan now is to treat it as a mechanical strain, keep you moving, and use the scan only if nerve symptoms appear, red flags develop, or you are not improving after about 6 weeks.
reply: Okay, I understand. I just want to know what's going on, but if staying active and the ibuprofen will help, I will give it a go.
